items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: you talk about Michelangelo’s “David” I mean it’s like the stone is there but he sees the thing.

ctx.x: And you had mentioned you have done some interviews with people about that, what they think of how they do it. And can you articulate what you’re thinking if you’re playing “Ain’t Misbehavin’” for instance, and you’re improvising over the changes, is there something — a thought process — that you can talk about?

Well it’s funny because I said I’ve done these interviews. I’ve never been interviewed myself on this subject. So I don’t, I’m just speaking off the top of my head. But from my own experience it’s the less thinking the better. The more you feel like you’re part of the whole group, and that the music is just kind of there, you’re just sort of pulling it out of the air, the better you are. And I have that feeling when I write too by the way, which is not that I am really creating it, but it’s like the thing is…

But I’ve heard it before, actually. Some people have used the word “Zen,” you know it’s a Zen experience. But I think the challenge with that is to try to relate that to younger players. Because some people, some of the veterans complain that the younger musicians
